title: AKP Deputy Chair Resigns as Ankara's $18bn Fund Crisis Turns Political; OECD Cuts Turkey Growth Outlook
subhead: Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya resigned from all AKP leadership posts over alleged stock trades tied to the collapsing investment-fund market, as 51 people were jailed and the OECD raised its inflation forecast for Turkey while trimming growth.

sections.heading: Fund Crisis Becomes a Political Crisis: AKP Deputy Chair Steps Down
sections.body:
AKP deputy chair and former family minister Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya announced late Saturday that she had asked Erdoğan to relieve her of all party positions, and party spokesman Ömer Çelik confirmed Sunday that the resignation was accepted, per AP and Turkish Minute. Kaya framed the move as taking 'political responsibility' so that the investigation into her share trades could proceed 'independently, impartially, and without any suspicion or undue influence.'

The allegations came from Zeynel Emre, spokesman for the opposition Yeni Party, who said on Sept. 26 that Kaya and her husband İlyas Kaya invested roughly 163 million lira (~$3.3m) in April, mainly in shipbuilder Özata Denizcilik, and later sold for about 2.17 billion lira (~$44m). Özata shares moved from ~220 lira in early April to 4,980 lira by Sept. 15 before the fund squeeze hit. Neither Kaya was named in the Capital Markets Board (SPK) criminal complaint over those trades, and no finding against them has been made — the regulatory action concerns separate suspects.
sections.whyItMatters: The crisis has moved from a market-liquidity problem to a ruling-party integrity problem. When a senior AKP figure resigns to protect an investigation, it signals the political cost is now being managed at the top, not contained at the regulator.

sections.heading: The Numbers Behind the Crisis: 131 Funds, 455,758 Investors, 51 Jailed
sections.body:
The SPK ordered the liquidation of 131 investment funds across seven portfolio companies (including Tera Portföy, Pusula Portföy and Hedef Portföy), with combined portfolios of roughly 891 billion lira. The Central Securities Depository put the number of affected individual investors at 455,758; the SPK earlier cited ~353,000. Per Turkish Minute and IBTimes, the trigger was an August tightening of SPK rules on funds' illiquid concentrated holdings; as funds sold to comply, redemptions snowballed. BIST 100 fell ~5.5% on Sept. 16 and more than 8% that week — its worst since March 2025.

Enforcement has escalated. Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said assets of 46 legal entities, 18 investment funds and 42 individuals were frozen, with 37 suspects barred from leaving the country, and 51 people in pre-trial detention — including a former central bank deputy governor. On Sept. 21 the SPK extended the liquidation window from three to six months. Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek dismissed resignation rumors as 'baseless'; Erdoğan, speaking in New York, said 'there is no risk to either our financial system or the Turkish economy.'
sections.whyItMatters: The headline dollar figure (~$18bn) understates the political blast radius: hundreds of thousands of retail investors are now directly exposed, and the detained ex-central-bank official ties the scandal to the institution most responsible for market credibility.

sections.heading: Economy: OECD Sharply Raises Turkey Inflation Forecast, Trims Growth
sections.body:
Reuters reported that the OECD raised its 2026 and 2027 inflation forecasts for Turkey and cut its growth projections for both years — a double downgrade that lands as the fund crisis tests confidence in Turkish financial markets. Separately, sovereign strategist Timothy Ash wrote (via AFP) that Turkey 'can absorb its $15bn–20bn investment fund collapse without a systemic crisis as long as Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek stays,' while calling for a full investigation into 'what went wrong, who was responsible, and reforms enacted.'

The IMF-adjacent FATF also said Turkey had strengthened its anti-money-laundering and terrorist-financing regime but still needs more work on tracing cross-border criminal proceeds and recovering illicit assets (Reuters, Sept. 23).
sections.whyItMatters: The OECD revision removes the easy 'temporary and manageable' framing the Financial Stability Committee used. The market's stabilizing anchor is now explicitly tied to one minister remaining in place — a single-point-of-failure the government cannot easily deny.

sections.heading: Defense: Turkey Offers Saudi Arabia Early-Warning and Air-Defense Help at Mecca Pact Meeting
sections.body:
At the Mecca Defense Alliance meeting in Riyadh, Turkish Chief of General Staff Gen. Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu proposed assisting Saudi Arabia's defenses against Houthi missile and drone attacks, per ssbulten. The offer covered early-warning systems, radar and sensor networks, electronic warfare, air defense and integrated command-and-control. Ankara attached a clear condition: no direct military confrontation with Iran.

The trilateral alliance (Turkey–Pakistan–Saudi Arabia) has stood up a strategic committee in Istanbul and a secretariat in Riyadh, with Pakistani official Nauman Mahmood appointed its first Secretary General. Saudi Arabia has not yet formally requested support; separately, under a 2023 export agreement, 15 Saudi pilots and 15 technicians have completed Bayraktar AKINCI UAV training at Çorlu.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is converting a political pact into a concrete defense-industrial role in the Gulf without crossing into direct confrontation with Iran — expanding influence in Riyadh while protecting its Iran relationship. It is a template for how Ankara sells capability without picking a side.

sections.heading: Iraq and the Bashiqa Handover: Turning a Withdrawal into Leverage
sections.body: Following the Sept. 23 agreement — announced after Erdoğan–Iraqi talks in New York — for Turkey to gradually hand over its Bashiqa-Zilkan military camp in northern Iraq to Baghdad, and to end the presence of 'outlawed armed elements' in northern Iraq (Reuters), Al-Monitor assessed that Ankara hopes the handover will deepen security cooperation with Baghdad and unlock broader bilateral gains. The deal extends Iraqi state authority in the Sinjar area while leaving Turkey with a negotiated foothold rather than a unilateral one.
sections.whyItMatters: Ankara is trading a fixed base for a durable role inside a Baghdad-endorsed framework. The reference to 'outlawed armed elements' gives Turkey a face-saving path on the PKK question in Iraq without an open-ended occupation.

sections.heading: Kurdish Peace Process: A Law Dissolving the PKK, and Wary Public Hope
sections.body: Telegraph and Yahoo reporting focus on the parliamentary law passed recently to dissolve the armed PKK and rehabilitate those involved in the conflict, as Kurds in the southeast meet Erdoğan's peace deal 'with hope and trepidation.' The coverage stresses that the process is real but still contested on the ground — the legal framework is advancing faster than the social trust.
sections.whyItMatters: The disarmament track is now backed by legislation rather than just a political declaration, which raises the cost of reversal for all parties — but implementation, not the vote, will determine whether the process holds.

sections.heading: Nuclear Debate Reopens as Iran War Reframes Turkey's Options
sections.body: A Cyprus Mail analysis (Sept. 28) asks whether the Iran war has changed Turkey's nuclear calculus, noting the country's long-standing atomic ambitions tracing back to Eisenhower's 1955 'Atoms for Peace.' The piece is analytically cautious: it treats the debate as reopened by regional instability rather than as a decision Ankara has made. No policy change has been announced.
sections.whyItMatters: Worth flagging only as a signal, not a shift: the war has revived a dormant argument about Turkey's nuclear hedging. No verified policy moves exist yet — treat speculation accordingly.

bottomLine: The day's dominant story is political, not market: a sitting AKP deputy chair resigned over share trades tied to the $18bn investment-fund collapse, while 51 people sit in pre-trial detention and 455,758 investors face liquidations. Paired with the OECD's inflation upgrade and growth downgrade, the crisis is now testing both the government's economic credibility and its internal discipline. Simsek's tenure has become the market's stated backstop, which is exactly the kind of single-point dependency Ankara cannot afford. On the external front, Turkey is methodically converting pacts into presence — an air-defense offer to Riyadh under the Mecca alliance, a negotiated Iraq base handover — expanding regional role while carefully avoiding direct confrontation with Iran.
sources: AP News, Reuters, Turkish Minute, AFP (via Turkish Minute), IBTimes Singapore, Yahoo News (Turkish Minute), Al-Monitor, Telegraph, ssbulten.com.tr, Cyprus Mail, FATF (via Reuters), OECD (via Reuters)
